title: CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO. On Fate
latin: CAPUT TRICESIMUM SECUNDUM, De Fato. FATUM est magnus divinae sapientiae influxus largiens rebus modum, quo in causando ad se invicem ordinantur. SECUNDUS ergo magnus influxus rebus inditus est Fatum, differens a necessitate, quae potissimum consistere videtur in rebus simplicibus et solitarie consideratis, eo quod ipsum fatum videtur esse in rerum multarum concursu, et pertinere ad sapientiam ordinantem, sicuti necessitas ad potentiam dantem unicuique esse iuxta modum suum. Unde fatum dicitur a fando, teste B. Augustino, quasi quae fato fiunt, ab aliquo dicente ac iubente ordinata ac decreta sint. Sed tamen nomen fati explodendum putat, quia dicit hoc datum esse sideribus ab Astrologis, in quo ei adstipulatur D. Gregorius. Quin etiam philosophi antiquiores, qui Deo generationem mundi et distinctionem regimenque rerum dederunt, fati nomen vanum esse falsumque dicunt, ut Anaxagoras, teste Alexandro libro de Fato et secundo de anima; et in sacra Scriptura non invenies nomen Fati, etiamsi sors, casus et fortuna inibi interdum inveniatur.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): even if lot, chance plus fortune are sometimes found therein — plus in sacred Scripture you will not find ye name Fate — as Anaxagoras, with Alexander witnessing in ye book concerning Fate plus ye second concerning ye soul — who gave God ye world's generation plus ye distinction plus regimen belonging toward things — Moreover even more ancient philosophers say ye name belonging toward fate is vain plus false. in which Doctor Gregory agrees with him — because he says this was given toward ye stars by Astrologers — But yet he thinks ye name belonging toward fate is to be exploded. as if those things which happen by fate were ordered plus decreed by someone speaking plus commanding — Whence fate is said from speaking, with Blessed Augustine witnessing. as necessity toward power giving each one to be according toward its mode — plus to pertain toward ordering wisdom — because fate itself seems to be in ye concurrence belonging toward many things — differing from necessity which seems chiefly to consist in simple things plus things considered alone. Therefore ye SECOND great influx put into things is Fate. FATE is ye great influx belonging toward divine wisdom granting things a mode by which in causing they are ordered toward one another. CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO. On Fate.
english: FATE is the great influx of divine wisdom granting things a mode by which in causing they are ordered toward one another. Therefore the SECOND great influx put into things is Fate, differing from necessity — which seems chiefly to consist in simple things considered alone — inasmuch as fate itself seems to be in the concurrence of many things and to pertain to ordering wisdom, as necessity pertains to power giving each thing to be according to its mode.

Whence fate is said from speaking (fari), as Blessed Augustine witnesses, as if the things that happen by fate were ordered and decreed by someone speaking and commanding. Yet he thinks the name of fate ought to be exploded, because he says this was given to the stars by the Astrologers — in which Doctor Gregory agrees with him. Moreover even the more ancient philosophers who gave God the world's generation and the distinction and regimen of things say the name of fate is vain and false, as Anaxagoras, Alexander witnessing in the book On Fate and the second On the Soul; and in sacred Scripture you will not find the name Fate, even if lot, chance, and fortune are sometimes found there.

title: Scripture attributes to God what some call fate; atheist and Machiavellian abuse of fate
latin: Quae enim a Theologis et Philosophis quibusdam fato tribuuntur, Moses tribuit Deo, cum dicit Exodus 21:12–13: Si quis occiderit hominem nolens sponte sua, sed quia delapsa est securis, occidit eum, quia Dominus tradidit illum in manum eius. Verum enimvero Alexander ait, qui negat nomen Fati, reclamat communi credulitati et usui loquendi. Idcirco non est fide dignus. Sed patres non credulitati verae sed falsae reclamant, et non tollunt nomen Fati nisi ubi fallaciae periculum in intellectu sit. Anxie autem disquirunt quid sit fatum et philosophi, et communis opinio est quod sit ordo causarum. Homerus quidem et Ovidius introducunt Jovem librantem fata et non potentem praeter fatum quid facere. Haec eadem saepe inculcant hodie Machiavellistae et Athei nostri temporis, quod si vere, inquiunt, Deus dat leges, tamen eas non observamus quodam fato aliud agentes; et cum nos punire vult non potest. Sic athei praetextu Fati arcana religionis Christianae corrumpunt.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): so atheists under ye pretext belonging toward Fate corrupt ye secrets belonging toward Christian religion. plus when he wills to punish us he cannot — yet we do not observe them acting something else by a certain fate — that if truly, they say, God gives laws — These same things today's Machiavellists plus Atheists belonging toward our time often inculcate. Homer indeed plus Ovid introduce Jupiter weighing fates plus not able to do anything beside fate. plus ye common opinion is that it is ye order belonging toward causes — But anxiously philosophers also inquire what fate is. Exodus 21:12–13 — For those things which by some Theologians plus Philosophers are attributed toward fate, Moses attributes toward God.
english: For what some theologians and philosophers attribute to fate, Moses attributes to God when he says (Exodus 21:12–13): If anyone kills a man not willing it of his own accord, but because the axe slipped, he killed him because the Lord delivered him into his hand. Yet Alexander says that whoever denies the name of Fate cries out against common credulity and usage of speech, and therefore is not worthy of faith. But the fathers cry out not against true but against false credulity, and they do not take away the name of Fate except where there is danger of fallacy in the intellect.

And philosophers anxiously inquire what fate is, and the common opinion is that it is an order of causes. Homer and Ovid indeed introduce Jupiter weighing the fates and unable to do anything beside fate. These same things today's Machiavellists and atheists of our time often press — that if God truly gives laws, yet we do not keep them, acting otherwise by a certain fate; and when He wills to punish us He cannot. So atheists under the pretext of Fate corrupt the secrets of the Christian religion.

title: Chaldeans, Peripatetics, Astrologers, Aquinas, and Boethius on fate's mutability
latin: Chaldaei et Aegyptii sapientes putarunt fatum sacrificiis et orationibus mutari posse, quia Deus ordinator rerum non ligaverit sibi manus ne possit facere aliud quam ab aeterno decreverit. Peripatetici hanc mutationem in Deo non admittunt, sed potius quaedam praeter eius intellectum et voluntatem a casu fieri ex concursu causarum inferiorum, et posse a nostro arbitrio et a fortuna fati seriem rescindi. Hoc negant Astrologi, quia omnis causa per accidens reducitur ad superiorem causam per se: unde series fati infallibilis videtur Arabibus apud Averroem, et nominatim Avicennae cum Stoicis contra Aristotelem. Thomas Aquinas lectione 3 in sextum Metaphysicorum putat Aristotelis rationem nec fatum tollere nec providentiam, et esse fallacem quia respicit causas particulares non universales, id quod et Boethius docet exemplo duorum servorum. Ponenda autem est triplex causa: 1. universalissima eaque immutabilis ut Deus; 2. universalis sed mutabilis ut caelum; 3. particularis ad proprios effectus ordinata.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): 3. particular ordered toward proper effects — 2. universal but mutable as heaven — 1. ye most universal plus immutable as God — But a triple cause is to be posited. which also Boethius teaches by ye example belonging toward two servants — Thomas Aquinas in lecture 3 on ye sixth of ye Metaphysics thinks Aristotle's reason neither takes away fate nor providence. whence ye series belonging toward fate seems infallible toward ye Arabs at Averroes, plus namely toward Avicenna with ye Stoics against Aristotle — Astrologers deny this. Peripatetics do not admit this mutation in God. Chaldean plus Egyptian wise men thought fate can be changed by sacrifices plus prayers.
english: The Chaldean and Egyptian wise men thought fate can be changed by sacrifices and prayers, because God the orderer of things did not bind His own hands so that He cannot do other than He decreed from eternity. The Peripatetics do not admit this mutation in God, but rather that some things happen by chance beside His intellect and will from the concurrence of inferior causes, and that the series of fate can be cut by our choice and by fortune.

Astrologers deny this, because every accidental cause is reduced to a superior cause of itself: whence the series of fate seems infallible to the Arabs in Averroes, and namely to Avicenna with the Stoics against Aristotle. Thomas Aquinas (lecture 3 on Metaphysics VI) thinks Aristotle's reason neither takes away fate nor providence, and is fallacious because it regards particular causes, not universal — which Boethius also teaches by the example of two servants. And a triple cause is to be posited: (1) the most universal and immutable, as God; (2) universal but mutable, as heaven; (3) particular, ordered to its proper effects.

title: Not all effects reduce to heaven; soul, angels, demons; contingent modification
latin: Sed quia non omnes effectus ad caelum possunt reduci, remanent adhuc alia contingentia respectu caeli. Primo, quia animae humanae, angeli et daemones intra ordinem rerum concausantium, teste Augustino et Boethio, non subduntur caelo nisi per accidens, quatenus anima corporibus alligata per organa affecta secundum sensum afficitur — et ipsae possunt dominari sensui, reprimendo iram, excutiendo pigritiam, et percipiendo remedia contra pestem et alios letiferos caeli influxus, et adiuvando occultis modis seipsas per preces ad Deum fusas. Idcirco non omnis caeli effectus est necessarius. Deinde, quia materia in quam agit caelum est vario modo disposita, aliterque suscipit actionem caeli validam et necessariam, aliter imbecillam et contingentem, ut patet ex meteorologia. Ergo licet in caelo siderum aspectus sint necessario, tamen ex defectibilitate inferiorum modificantur ad contingentiam.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): yet from ye defectibility belonging toward inferiors they are modified toward contingency — Therefore although in heaven ye aspects belonging toward stars are necessary. as is plain from meteorology — otherwise weak plus contingent — plus otherwise it receives heaven's action strong plus necessary — Next, because ye matter into which heaven acts is disposed in a varied mode. therefore not every effect belonging toward heaven is necessary. plus helping themselves by hidden modes through prayers poured toward God — First, because human souls, angels plus demons within ye order belonging toward concausing things, with Augustine plus Boethius witnessing, are not subjected toward heaven except accidentally. But because not all effects can be reduced toward heaven, there remain still other contingencies with respect toward heaven.
english: But because not all effects can be reduced to heaven, other contingencies still remain with respect to heaven. First, because human souls, angels, and demons within the order of concausing things — as Augustine and Boethius witness — are not subjected to heaven except accidentally, inasmuch as the soul bound to bodies is affected through organs according to sense — and they themselves can master sense by repressing anger, shaking off sloth, perceiving remedies against plague and other deadly influxes of heaven, and helping themselves by hidden modes through prayers poured out to God. Therefore not every effect of heaven is necessary.

Next, because the matter on which heaven acts is variously disposed, and otherwise receives heaven's action as strong and necessary, otherwise as weak and contingent, as is plain from meteorology. Therefore although the aspects of the stars in heaven are necessary, yet from the defectibility of inferior things they are modified unto contingency.

title: Boethius: fate as disposition inhering in mobile things; Cap. 32 close toward harmony
latin: Ergo fatum, ut Boethius docet libro 4 de consolatione philosophiae, est rebus mobilibus inhaerens immobilis dispositio, per quam providentia suis quaeque nectit ordinibus. Non sequitur quod omnia eveniant necessario, sed esse necessarium quod effectus eveniant alii necessario, alii libere, alii contingenter, prout illis praeparavit causas Deus, cuius proprium est dare esse, aliarum vero est uti esse dato ad necessitatem vel contingentiam. Respectu caeli non datur fatum inevitabile, sed respectu causae universalissimae, cuius ordinem vocat providentiam et non fatum, ad quam pertinet facere omne ens sicuti est. Sic fatum sapientiae ordinantis praeparat transitum ad harmoniam, quae est magnus divini amoris influxus — de quo caput tricesimum tertium.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): concerning which ye thirty-third chapter — which is ye great influx belonging toward divine love — So fate belonging toward ordering wisdom prepares ye passage toward harmony. toward which it pertains to make every being as it is — whose order he calls providence plus not fate — but with respect toward ye most universal cause — With respect toward heaven inevitable fate is not given. whose proper is to give being, but belonging toward others is to use being given toward necessity or contingency — as God prepared causes toward them — but that it is necessary that effects happen some necessarily, others freely, others contingently. It does not follow that all things happen necessarily. through which providence binds each things toward its orders — Fate, as Boethius teaches in book 4 concerning ye consolation belonging toward philosophy, is an immobile disposition inhering in mobile things.
english: Therefore fate, as Boethius teaches in book 4 of the Consolation of Philosophy, is an immobile disposition inhering in mobile things, through which providence binds each thing to its orders. It does not follow that all things happen necessarily, but that it is necessary that some effects happen necessarily, others freely, others contingently, according as God prepared causes for them — whose proper work is to give being, while others use being once given unto necessity or contingency.

With respect to heaven inevitable fate is not given, but with respect to the most universal cause, whose order he calls providence and not fate, to which it pertains to make every being as it is. So fate of ordering wisdom prepares the passage to harmony, which is the great influx of divine love — of which the thirty-third chapter.
